items.quote: brought it back to his own city to mourn for him and bury him. Then he laid the body in his own tomb
items.contrast: The body is taken to the city first and placed in the tomb afterward.
items.reason: The tomb is a plausible later destination, but the explicit sequence establishes the prophet’s own city as the first destination.

items.quote: So let’s go over to the camp of the Arameans and surrender.
items.contrast: Going into the city is a rejected possibility; going to the Aramean camp to surrender is the decision.
items.reason: The men consider entering the city but say that it would also result in death. “So let’s” clearly introduces their actual decision.

items.quote: made a covenant between the Lord and the king and people that they would be the Lord’s people.
items.contrast: The first covenant includes the Lord, king, and people; the second is only between the king and people.
items.reason: The passage names two covenants in sequence, so identifying the first requires keeping their participants distinct.

items.quote: brought their scrolls together and burned them publicly.
items.contrast: They burn the gathered scrolls before the scrolls’ value is calculated.
items.reason: The sequence uniquely supports public burning. However, “assembling materials” is an avoidably generic description of bringing their scrolls together; the stem should name the scrolls directly.

items.quote: Should I give up my oil, by which both gods and humans are honored, to hold sway over the trees?
items.contrast: The olive tree refuses because ruling would mean giving up its honored oil, not because the trees subsequently approach the fig tree.
items.reason: The olive tree’s rhetorical question directly gives its reason. The move to the fig tree occurs afterward and cannot explain the olive tree’s refusal.
